title: Annotated Equations
order: 4
---

A quick reference for the models introduced in the [R Tutorial](r_tutorial.qmd).

## Baseline model: AR + covariate + Gaussian error

The same structure as the ARIMAX models from previous lessons: a covariate, an AR term, and Gaussian error.

$$
y_t = \underbrace{\color{#2b6cb0}{c}}_{\textstyle\color{#2b6cb0}{\text{constant}}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#319795}{\beta_1 x_{1,t}}}_{\textstyle\color{#319795}{\text{covariate}}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#c05621}{\beta_2 y_{t-1}}}_{\textstyle\color{#c05621}{\text{AR: lag-1}}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#718096}{\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)}}_{\textstyle\color{#718096}{\text{Gaussian noise}}}
$$

- $y_t$ — the observed value at time $t$
- $c$ — a constant
- $\beta_1 x_{1,t}$ — the covariate effect
- $\beta_2 y_{t-1}$ — AR: the effect of the previous value
- $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ — Gaussian noise with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2$

**In `mvgam`:** the AR term is specified with `trend_model = AR(p = 1)` rather than in the model formula.

## The same model, decomposed

The same model written as an observation distribution around a modeled mean.

$$
y_t = \mathcal{N}(
  \underbrace{\color{#d53f8c}{\mu_t}}_{\textstyle\color{#d53f8c}{\text{process mean}}},\sigma^2
)
$$

$$
\color{#d53f8c}{\mu_t} = \underbrace{\color{#2b6cb0}{c}}_{\textstyle\color{#2b6cb0}{\text{constant}}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#319795}{\beta_1 x_{1,t}}}_{\textstyle\color{#319795}{\text{covariate}}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#c05621}{\beta_2 y_{t-1}}}_{\textstyle\color{#c05621}{\text{AR: lag-1}}}
$$

- $y_t$ — the observed value at time $t$, drawn from a normal distribution
- $\mu_t$ — the process mean at time $t$
- $\sigma^2$ — the variance of the noise around that mean
- $c$, $\beta_1 x_{1,t}$, $\beta_2 y_{t-1}$ — the same terms as the baseline model, now determining $\mu_t$

**Why rewrite it:** separating the observation distribution from the model of $\mu_t$ makes it easy to swap in a different distribution.

## Modeling count data: Poisson error

Counts are non-negative integers, so we replace the normal distribution with a Poisson distribution.

$$
y_t = \mathrm{Pois}(
  \underbrace{\color{#d53f8c}{\lambda_t}}_{\textstyle\color{#d53f8c}{\text{rate parameter}}}
)
$$

$$
\underbrace{\color{#d69e2e}{\log(\lambda_t)}}_{\textstyle\color{#d69e2e}{\text{log link}}} = \underbrace{\color{#2b6cb0}{c}}_{\textstyle\color{#2b6cb0}{\text{constant}}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#319795}{\beta_1 x_{1,t}}}_{\textstyle\color{#319795}{\text{covariate}}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\color{#c05621}{\beta_2 y_{t-1}}}_{\textstyle\color{#c05621}{\text{AR: lag-1}}}
$$

- $y_t$ — the observed count at time $t$
- $\lambda_t$ — the Poisson rate parameter: both the mean and the variance, so it must be positive
- $\log(\lambda_t)$ — the log link: modeling $\log(\lambda_t)$ instead of $\lambda_t$ keeps $\lambda_t$ positive
- $c$, $\beta_1 x_{1,t}$, $\beta_2 y_{t-1}$ — the same terms as before, now predicting $\log(\lambda_t)$

**Note:** the model is linear on the log scale, so the covariate's effect on untransformed abundance is exponential.
